title: Emulating non-Markovian system-bath dynamics with parametrically driven cavities
authors: Valentin Boettcher, Félix Pellerin, Philippe St-Jean, William A. Coish
abstract: We introduce and characterize a scheme for emulating non-Markovian quantum system-bath dynamics using the discrete electromagnetic field modes of a parametrically driven cavity. In this scheme, the character of a bosonic bath (the form of the bath spectral density) is tied directly to the shape of the real-time waveform describing periodic parametric cavity modulation. As an explicit example, we demonstrate the feasibility of this scheme for a fiber-loop experiment with currently achievable parameters, supported by numerical simulations and analytical estimates. In particular, we show that a localization transition of the spin-boson model can be accurately emulated in this fiber-loop cavity system. This localization effect is characterized by a sharp transition from partial decay to complete decay for a two-level system coupled to a bosonic bath as the bath spectral density $J(ω)\propto ω^{s}$ is continously tuned from the sub-ohmic ($s<1$) to the super-ohmic ($s>1$) regime. The transition is only exactly realized in the thermodynamic limit (for an infinite number of bath modes) and for sufficiently weak system-bath coupling. We highlight a competition between the weak-coupling and thermodynamic limits in this problem and show that challenges in approximately realizing the transition can nevertheless be overcome. Finally, we provide bounds on the systematic error introduced when emulating non-Markovian dynamics for arbitrary system observables. The scheme presented here can enable the realization of a modular platform for engineering custom non-Markovian baths, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics, thermalization of many-body systems, and resource-efficient quantum simulations of open quantum systems.
summary: This paper presents a method to engineer complex, non-Markovian quantum baths using the controlled modulation of a parametric optical cavity. By tuning the modulation waveform, the bath spectral density can be continuously controlled, allowing for the accurate simulation of phenomena like the spin-boson localization transition. This offers a modular platform for fundamental studies in open quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately simulating non-Markovian quantum system-bath dynamics, which standard Markovian approximations fail to capture.
main_result: They demonstrate a novel, highly tunable platform using parametrically driven cavities to emulate arbitrary non-Markovian bath spectral densities, specifically realizing the localization transition of the spin-boson model.
method: The method involves engineering the bath spectral density $J(\omega)$ by controlling the real-time modulation waveform of a cavity, which is modeled as a synthetic long-range hopping system.
model_or_system: The physical system is a quantum system coupled to a bath realized by the discrete electromagnetic modes of a parametrically driven optical cavity (fiber-loop). The underlying model is the spin-boson model, whose bath coupling is engineered via the cavity's modulation.
key_observables: The decay probability $p_e(	au)$ of a two-level system, and the bath correlation function $c(	au)$.
important_parameters: The spectral exponent $s$ governing the bath spectral density $J(\omega) \propto \omega^s$, which can be tuned continuously from sub-ohmic ($s<1$) to super-ohmic ($s>1$).
main_assumptions: The exact realization requires the thermodynamic limit (infinite bath modes) and assumes the validity of approximations related to the nonstationary phase evolution.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the setup (System coupled to a modulated cavity bath), and Figure 2 shows the decay probability $p_e(	au)$ for different spectral regimes ($s<1$ vs $s>1$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the scheme, details the Hamiltonian and the mechanism for tuning $J(\omega)$ via the cavity's synthetic dimension, demonstrates the emulation of the spin-boson localization transition, and concludes with theoretical bounds on systematic errors.
why_interesting: This work provides an experimentally accessible, highly tunable platform for engineering structured quantum environments, which is crucial for advancing quantum thermodynamics and open quantum system research.
